items.prompt: Define motivation.
items.canonical_answer: Motivation is the willingness of an employee to work hard towards the business's goals because the work, the rewards or the surroundings give the worker a reason to do so.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must cover willingness to work towards the business's goals and the reason behind it. Saying workers are happy is not a definition.

items.prompt: The machinists at a Windhoek garment factory are paid by the piece, say they work "for the money and nothing else", and their output has stopped rising. Explain how meeting the non-money needs of these workers could lead to better results for the business.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the starting point is workers whose pay already rises with effort, so money alone has stopped pushing output. Mechanism: because pay now covers their basic needs, the needs that could still move them are the non-money ones - workmates, recognition, the sense of getting better at the job - and meeting these through teamworking, praise or training gives effort a second reason to exist. Consequence: the likely effect is machinists who care about quality and output for its own sake, so productivity rises, fewer leave, and the business keeps its experienced hands and its reputation with buyers. The stakeholder group that gains alongside the owners is the machinists themselves, whose working day becomes more satisfying at the same wage.
marking_guidance: Condition: the mechanism must be tied to the given starting point of effort that pay alone has stopped moving.
Mechanism: award for the why or how - once basic needs are met it is the non-money needs that can still motivate, because pay has become background.
Consequence: award for the effect or result for the business - productivity, retention and quality.
Objective: award for naming who gains - the business and its workers as the stakeholder group.

items.prompt: Tulime Garden Services in Otjiwarongo pays its 14 workers a fixed monthly salary. The owner has noticed that work quality falls whenever she is out of the nursery. Explain what is likely to be happening to motivation at Tulime, and what the owner should do about it.
items.canonical_answer: The context facts - fixed monthly pay and effort that slips when unobserved - suggest the workers currently work for the money alone, so their effort stops where supervision stops. That is a motivation gap rather than a discipline problem: the pay need is met, but no other need, such as recognition or growing skill, is being fed by the work. The reasoning: with pay fixed and effort unwatched, neither money nor pride currently rewards extra care. Conclusion: the owner should add a reason to work well that does not depend on her presence - for example, letting small teams take responsibility for the gardens they serve, with the team's name on the job and a small bonus for client praise - so quality is driven by the workers' own motivation rather than by her watching.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the named business's facts - fixed monthly pay and quality falling when the owner is absent.
Reasoning: award for the link between fixed pay without supervision and low effort, because no reward beyond the salary reaches these workers.
Conclusion: award a choice for this business that follows the reasoning, such as team responsibility with recognition.

items.prompt: Explain the main features of the reasons why people work.
items.canonical_answer: The main features come in two parts. Money: wages and salaries pay for the needs and wants of a household - food, rent, school fees - and for most people work is the source of that money. Beyond money: people also work for the satisfaction of doing a job well, for the company of workmates, for the status a role carries, and for a sense of achievement when a target is met. A further feature is that the balance shifts: where pay is too low to live on, money dominates the reasons, whereas once the basics are covered the non-money reasons grow in weight - so the mix differs from person to person and from situation to situation.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - pay for needs and wants, satisfaction, the company of colleagues, status and achievement - and for what the pattern includes: the mix shifts as pay moves from scarce to adequate.

items.prompt: Define labour turnover.
items.canonical_answer: Labour turnover is the rate at which employees leave a business over a period, usually expressed as a percentage of the total workforce that has to be replaced each year.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must express leaving as a rate or percentage of the workforce over a period. Naming people leaving alone is not a definition.

items.prompt: Explain why a well-motivated workforce tends to benefit a business.
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that motivated workers care about the result of their work, and that care shows up in the three measures. Because they want the outcome, they produce more per worker - higher labour productivity. Because they want to be part of the work, they turn up - lower absenteeism. Because leaving means giving up something they value, they stay - lower labour turnover. The purpose of the benefit is cumulative: higher output per worker tends to lower the cost of each unit, and fewer leavers mean the business spends less on advertising vacancies, interviewing and training replacements while keeping the skill it has already paid for.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the link - caring about outcomes raises productivity, attendance and staying - because effort follows motivation, not just presence.
Second reason: award for the purpose side of the benefit - lower cost per unit and less spending on replacements.

items.prompt: Explain the features of labour productivity as a measure of how well a workforce is performing.
items.canonical_answer: Labour productivity is the output each worker produces in a given period, such as crates per packer per day. Its features: it compares output with the people who produced it, so it rises when workers produce more or when the same output needs fewer workers; it is usually measured over a period, so a single busy day proves little; and it says nothing about why the figure stands where it does - better training, better machines or longer hours all lift it - so a manager reads it alongside absenteeism and labour turnover before concluding anything about motivation.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - output per worker per period, and rising when output per person rises - and for what it includes as a caution: the measure alone does not reveal the cause of a change.

items.prompt: Define Maslow's hierarchy of human needs.
items.canonical_answer: Maslow's hierarchy is the idea that human needs arrange themselves in levels, from basic physiological needs at the bottom to self-actualisation at the top, and that a lower level generally has to be reasonably satisfied before the next level up motivates a person's behaviour.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include needs arranged in levels, with lower ones met before higher ones motivate. Listing the five levels alone is not the definition.

items.prompt: Explain why, according to Maslow, a worker whose pay is comfortable may be unmoved by a further pay increase.
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that a satisfied need no longer motivates. Because the worker's physiological and safety needs are already met by the existing wage, a further increase lands on needs that are already satisfied, so it adds little drive. What would motivate instead is the next level up - social belonging, esteem, recognition, or the chance to take on work that grows the worker's potential. This is why businesses whose pay is already at the market level often get more movement from responsibility, praise and promotion than from another small allowance.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the satisfied need no longer motivating, because motivation pulls from levels that are still unsatisfied.
Second reason: award for naming what would work instead - the higher levels, such as recognition or growth.

items.prompt: Explain the main features of the levels in Maslow's hierarchy of needs.
items.canonical_answer: The hierarchy has these parts, from the bottom: physiological needs - food, water, warmth and rest; safety needs - security of income, health and person; social needs - friendship, family and belonging at work; esteem needs - recognition, respect and status; and self-actualisation - the drive to reach one's full potential through challenging work. Two features hold the model together: each level has to be reasonably satisfied before the one above it starts to motivate, and pay with safe conditions serves the lower levels while recognition, responsibility and growth serve the upper ones.
marking_guidance: Features: award for the elements of each level, and for what the model includes: lower levels met before higher ones begin to motivate.

items.prompt: Define what Herzberg meant by a hygiene factor.
items.canonical_answer: A hygiene factor is an element of the job - such as pay, working conditions or job security - whose absence or weakness causes dissatisfaction, but whose presence does not create motivation: it removes dissatisfaction without adding drive.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must name both directions - poor hygiene factors cause dissatisfaction, and good ones do not motivate. Giving only the examples is not a definition.

items.prompt: Identify the main features of Taylor's approach to motivation.
items.canonical_answer: Taylor's approach has these elements: workers are motivated mainly by money; work is divided into simple, repeated tasks; each task is studied and taught as the one fastest method; and pay is linked to output, often piece by piece, so more effort earns more pay.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each part - pay at the centre, simple repeated tasks, the studied best method, and pay linked to output.

items.prompt: Define profit sharing as a method of financial reward.
items.canonical_answer: Profit sharing is a financial reward in which workers receive a stated share of the business's profits in addition to their normal pay, so the reward rises and falls with how well the whole business performs.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must tie the payment to a share of profits and to business performance. Describing a bonus alone is not the definition.

items.prompt: Explain why a bonus paid for reaching a monthly sales target may motivate a shop assistant more than a small increase in basic salary would.
items.canonical_answer: The reason is visibility and connection. A bonus is earned by a specific achievement within the month, so the assistant can see the link between effort and reward, and the purpose behind the payment - the target - is clear and reachable. A small permanent rise in basic salary becomes part of normal pay once it is received, and normal pay tends to stop pulling, because the worker adjusts to it as the new baseline. The bonus keeps its effect because it has to be earned again every month, whereas the salary rise is banked and gradually treated as ordinary.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the effort-reward link a target creates, because the worker can act on it within the month.
Second reason: award for the salary rise losing pull once it is treated as normal pay.

items.prompt: Explain the main features of the financial methods a business can use to reward its workers.
items.canonical_answer: The financial methods are these: a wage, paid by the hour or day for time worked; a salary, a fixed sum per month or year whatever the hours; a bonus, an extra payment for reaching a target; commission, a share of the value of each sale; and profit sharing, a stated share of the business's profits. What the set includes is a range of connections between pay and performance - from no link, for a salary, to a tight link, for commission - and a range of costs to the business, from predictable monthly sums to rewards that move with results.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - wage, salary, bonus, commission and profit sharing - and for what the set includes: differing strengths of link between pay and performance.

items.prompt: Define job enrichment.
items.canonical_answer: Job enrichment is a non-financial method in which a job is redesigned to give the worker more responsibility, challenge and variety - such as planning the work and checking its quality, not just performing it - so the work itself becomes more satisfying.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include redesign of the job with added responsibility and challenge. Describing job rotation instead is not the definition.

items.prompt: Explain how job rotation could benefit a business whose assembly workers complain that the work is monotonous.
items.canonical_answer: The developed benefit: rotation moves each worker between different tasks on a schedule, so no shift is a full day of one repeated motion. Because sameness is the complaint, the change strikes its cause, so workers are likely to find the day less dull and to stay motivated for longer, which leads to lower absenteeism and fewer leavers. For the business this leads to a wider benefit: workers who have rotated across the tasks can cover an absent colleague, so the line keeps running, and the business keeps the workers it has already trained instead of meeting the cost of replacing them.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for the variety removing the cause of boredom, because sameness was the complaint, developed further to the consequence it leads to - lower absenteeism, cover for absence and retained trained workers.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of using job enrichment to improve motivation.
items.canonical_answer: A developed limitation: enrichment adds responsibility and challenge, but not every worker wants them. A worker whose main aim is a steady day's pay for a steady day's work may experience the added planning and checking as pressure rather than growth, because more responsibility can feel like more risk of blame. That leads to the consequence that effort and satisfaction fall for exactly the people the method was meant to lift. There is also a practical limit: redesigning jobs and training workers for the wider role takes management time and money, so the benefits arrive slowly, and a business expecting a quick change is likely to be disappointed.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for the mismatch with workers who do not want added responsibility, because pressure can outweigh growth, developed to the consequence it leads to - dissatisfaction for some and slow, costly results for the business.

items.prompt: Ongwediva Electronics assembles radios with 30 workers, each doing one task all day. Pay is at the market rate. Workers are leaving, and exit interviews show the reason is boredom, not pay. Explain which method of motivation the manager should choose here, and why.

The reasoning: since pay already matches the market, a rise would work on a need that the exit interviews say is not the problem. The method that fits is job rotation, moving workers between the assembly tasks, because the named cause is a full day of one repeated motion, and rotation attacks exactly that. items.prompt: Explain the main features of teamworking as a method of motivation.
items.canonical_answer: Teamworking organises a group of workers around a shared goal with shared responsibility for the result. Its features: membership of a team meets social needs at work, because people do not want to let their workmates down; the team's success gives each member a share of achievement; and responsibility for the outcome is spread, so workers feel trusted with decisions rather than instructed. What it includes on the cost side is coordination - someone must set the goal and the team's boundaries - and the risk of free-riding, where a member lets the others carry the effort.
marking_guidance: Features: award for the elements - shared goal, shared responsibility, social belonging, shared achievement - and for what it includes as a caution: the risk of free-riding within the team.

items.prompt: Define what it means to match a method of motivation to given circumstances.
items.canonical_answer: Matching a method of motivation to given circumstances means diagnosing the actual cause of the low motivation - pay, boredom, missing recognition or the absence of a promotion path - and choosing the method that reaches that cause in this business's situation, rather than applying a reward that fits a different problem or a different budget.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include diagnosing the cause and choosing the method that answers it in this situation. Recommending a pay rise generically is not a definition.

items.prompt: The manager of Otavi Packaging, which employs 60 workers at the market rate of pay, proposes an across-the-board rise of N$250 a month for every worker to fix falling effort. Consider whether you would recommend this rise for this business.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: I would not recommend the across-the-board rise as it stands; a smaller, targeted change is the better recommendation - but the verdict depends on the cause of the falling effort, which has not yet been diagnosed. Context: the facts of this business matter. Pay already sits at the market rate, so the rise raises cost without answering any identified need - 60 workers at N$250 a month is N$15 000 a month, a permanent N$180 000 a year, spent on effort that has fallen for reasons nobody has named. Criterion: what decides this is whether money is the cause; on the market-rate comparison, hygiene is unlikely to be the binding problem, and Herzberg's finding is that pay at this level tends to remove dissatisfaction without creating effort. Counterargument: the case for the rise is real - pay that falls behind rivals demotivates quickly, an across-the-board rise is simple and felt to be fair, and it may lift morale if workers feel undervalued next to peers elsewhere. Condition: the recommendation depends on the diagnosis - if pay is in fact behind the market, part of the rise should go through quickly; if interviews name boredom or recognition, the same money buys more as rotation, training and praise than as a blanket increase.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear verdict on the proposed rise.
Context: award for using this business's facts - market-rate pay, 60 workers, and the N$15 000 monthly cost of the rise.
Criterion: award for naming what decides it - whether money is the cause of the falling effort.
Counterargument: award for the strongest case on the other side - fairness and the risk of falling behind rivals.
Condition: award for the recommendation depending on the diagnosis and on pay relative to the market.

items.prompt: At Swakopmund Boat Tours, the six guides are paid well but see no future in the job: the owner's family fills every senior role. Two of the best guides have just resigned. Explain what the owner should do to motivate the remaining guides, and why.
items.canonical_answer: The context facts - good pay, no promotion path and resignations by the best guides - locate the cause above the money levels: the pay need is met, but esteem and the chance to grow are not, because no route upward exists. items.prompt: Explain the main elements a manager should weigh before recommending a method of motivation.
items.canonical_answer: The elements to weigh are these parts of the decision: first, the cause of the low motivation - low pay, monotonous work, missing recognition or no upward path - because the method must reach the cause to work; second, the needs of the particular workers, which differ from one worker to the next; third, what the business can afford, both now and in every later year the cost recurs; and fourth, the fit with the rest of the business, such as whether a promotion path exists for the promoted to walk. What a sound recommendation includes is the condition under which it holds: the chosen method, the reason it reaches the named cause, and the check that will show whether it worked.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - cause, workers' needs, affordability and fit with the business - and for what the recommendation includes: the condition under which it holds.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Giving the best mechanic at Katima Auto Repairs the job of training the apprentices is a hygiene factor, because it improves her working conditions." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is placing a motivator among the hygiene factors. In fact Herzberg split workplace factors into two sets that do different jobs. Hygiene factors - pay, working conditions, job security, the way the business is run - cause dissatisfaction when they are poor; improving them removes that dissatisfaction but, on Herzberg's account, does not create extra effort. Motivators - achievement, recognition, responsibility, interesting work, personal growth - are the factors that generate motivation. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the change removes something workers dislike or adds something they value in the work itself. Training the apprentices does not fix a grievance about the mechanic's surroundings, pay or security; it adds responsibility, recognition of her skill and a chance to grow, so it is a motivator. Fitting a fan in a hot workshop or repairing a leaking roof would improve her working conditions, a hygiene factor: such changes could end her complaints, but Herzberg would not expect them to make her work harder.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact responsibility is one of Herzberg's motivators, not a hygiene factor; working conditions are a hygiene factor, and adding responsibility does not change them.

A 6-mark answer explains what hygiene factors are and what improving them does, explains what motivators are and what they do, and gives the test that separates them - removing a dislike against adding something valued in the work - applied to the mechanic's new training role.

items.prompt: The owner of Tsumeb Bread Baking employs 20 workers and believes motivation is low, but the business cannot afford a pay rise this year. Write several linked points for the owner: state two methods that would cost the business little or nothing, each with a reason why it could raise motivation here, and note one risk that comes with each.
items.canonical_answer: Point: job rotation - moving bakers between mixing, shaping and oven work - costs no extra pay and could raise motivation here, because the complaint such rotation answers is monotonous work, and variety gives the day shape. Its risk: every baker needs training on each task, so quality may dip while skills even out. Point: recognition - naming the week's best batch and letting a baker lead the morning briefing - costs nothing, and could raise motivation because recognition meets the esteem needs a wage cannot reach. Its risk: praise that feels routine, or that always lands on the same favourites, can breed cynicism, so it must be earned and explained. Linking both to this bakery: with no budget for pay, the owner's workable levers are variety and recognition, and both act on needs the wage has already left unsatisfied.
marking_guidance: Point: award for each method stated, up to two.
Reason: award for the because behind each - variety answers monotony, and recognition meets esteem needs.
Context: award for applying each point to this bakery and its empty pay budget.

items.prompt: Rundu Furniture Works makes school desks with 40 workers. Output per worker has fallen from 25 desks a month to 22. Absenteeism has risen to 12 days a worker a year, and labour turnover reached 20 per cent - eight of the 40 workers left last year and had to be replaced. The operations manager proposes a permanent across-the-board bonus of N$200 a month for every worker, costing N$8 000 a month. Using these facts, consider whether the manager's proposal is the right response for Rundu Furniture Works.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: the bonus on its own is unlikely to be the right response; a smaller combined package is the better recommendation, and the facts point that way. Context: the facts of this business locate the cause. Nothing shows pay below the market, while the symptoms - output per worker down at 22 desks against 25, absence up at 12 days, turnover at 20 per cent with eight leavers - fit jobs that have become monotonous better than they fit a pay gap. Criterion: the decisive test is whether money is the cause, and on the evidence given it is not named; Herzberg's finding warns that pay tends to remove dissatisfaction without adding effort, so a permanent N$8 000 a month may buy quiet rather than output. Counterargument: the case for the bonus is real - it is simple, it reaches everyone in the same week, and if workers have quietly fallen behind rival wages, N$200 a month is cheaper than losing eight more trained makers in a year. Condition: the recommendation depends on the diagnosis the facts do not yet contain - if interviews name pay, part of the N$8 000 should go to a targeted rise; if they name boredom, the same money buys rotation and enrichment, methods whose effect does not fade the month after it is paid, provided the business measures the three indicators again after three months.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on the bonus.
Context: award for using the facts - 22 desks against 25, 12 days of absence, 20 per cent turnover, and the N$8 000 monthly cost.
Criterion: award for naming what decides it - whether money is the cause of the fall.
Counterargument: award for the case on the other side - speed, simplicity, and the cost of losing trained workers.
Condition: award for the recommendation depending on the diagnosis and on re-measuring the three indicators.

items.prompt: Plan, without writing the full answer, a response to this 12-mark task: "Paying workers more is the best way for a business to motivate its workforce." Consider this view. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the strongest case against your judgement, and the conditions your final recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, define the terms: motivation as the willingness to work towards the business's goals, and the claim on the table - that money outperforms every other lever. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: pay meets the lower needs directly and visibly; where wages are low or behind rivals, money is the fastest and fairest lever, and Taylor's work supports it. Paragraph 3, the case against: Herzberg found pay a hygiene factor whose effect fades once accepted as normal; Maslow's levels say money moves the bottom of the ladder and not the rest; and non-financial methods such as enrichment and rotation reach needs pay cannot. Paragraph 4, judgement: the view holds where pay is genuinely the unsatisfied need and fails once pay is adequate; the criterion is the cause of the low motivation, not the size of the budget. Paragraph 5, conditions: the recommendation depends on the diagnosis of that cause and on the business's ability to sustain the cost, because a permanent rise, once given, is hard to withdraw.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the plan must state the verdict the answer would reach.
Context: the plan must use facts about how motivation works - hygiene against motivators, lower against upper needs.
Criterion: the plan must name what decides the verdict - the cause of the low motivation.
Counterargument: the plan must include the strongest case against the view or the verdict.
Condition: the recommendation must depend on stated conditions - the diagnosis and the sustainability of the cost.

items.prompt: Tromso Fjord Processing, a fish-packing plant in northern Norway, pays above the local average and uses piece-rate pay for its 90 packers. The work is three repeated motions a shift inside a chilled hall. Turnover is high - 30 packers left last year - and the supervisor reports that new starters reach full speed quickly but leave within months. Analyse the situation and recommend what the plant should do.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the facts fit a textbook mismatch. Pay is above the local average and piece-rate, so the money levers are already pulled - the pay need is met and effort is already priced - yet workers still leave in numbers. The cause is therefore likely to sit above pay: three repeated motions in a chilled hall starve the social, esteem and growth needs, and Herzberg's hygiene-versus-motivator finding predicts exactly this pattern - pay good enough to recruit cannot hold people whose jobs offer nothing else. The reasoning from evidence: starters reaching full speed quickly and then leaving shows the plant teaches the motions fast and retains nothing, so the job is the problem, not the wage. Recommendation: redesign the work - rotate packers between the three motions and the hall's support tasks, form small teams responsible for a bay's output with the bay's name on it, and open a lead-packer role that trains and checks the others, so a visible path upward exists. Judgement: this combined package, not more pay, is the right call, because the criterion is the cause - repetition and missing recognition - which money does not reach. Counterargument: pay already recruits well and redesign takes management time; some packers may prefer simple work. Condition: the recommendation depends on genuine implementation - rotation must be real variety and teams must keep real responsibility - and on measuring turnover and output after three months, because a decorated version of the same three motions would change nothing.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on what the plant should do.
Context: award for using the facts - above-average piece-rate pay, 30 leavers, the repeated motions, fast learning then leaving.
Criterion: award for naming what decides it - the cause that money does not reach.
Counterargument: award for the case against the redesign - pay already recruits, redesign costs management time, and some workers may prefer simple work.
Condition: award for the recommendation depending on genuine implementation and re-measurement.
